auth.welcomeBody: Here pain is not debated — it is heard. We help you understand what is happening in your body and your life, calmly and with science, without rushing labels.
auth.name: What should we call you

onboarding.welcomeBody: A new approach to pain: seeing the nervous system, the mind, and everyday life as one fabric — not as loose pieces.
onboarding.painRealBody: If it has hurt for months, you are not exaggerating. Persistent pain can stay active even when tests look fine. It deserves explanation, care, and company — including pain psychotherapy when it fits.
onboarding.whatBody: We orient your pain profile (mechanisms, mood, stress, lifestyle pillars, and beliefs) so the next step makes sense. We do not deliver a definitive diagnosis.
onboarding.whatPsych: For many persistent-pain profiles, pain psychotherapy (e.g. CBT for pain) is often a useful part of care to work on fear, automatic thoughts, and function — without denying that pain is real.
onboarding.prefsNeuroHint: Larger text, more space, less motion.
onboarding.consentBody: By continuing, you accept that Neuropi is a screening and education tool. It does not replace professional care. If there is urgency, seek in-person help.
onboarding.consentAccept: I understand and want to continue
onboarding.beliefsAutoBody: When it hurts, the mind sometimes jumps to the worst. These questions orient (pain CBT inspired); they are not a diagnosis or the PCS scale.
onboarding.beliefsLimBody: Some beliefs can close useful doors. Exploring them calmly opens space for pain psychotherapy — without saying your pain is “in your head”.
onboarding.beliefsSoftCta: Working on these beliefs with a pain psychologist is often part of integrated care in persistent pain.
onboarding.beliefsDoneBody: You have a first map of thoughts and beliefs. You can start understanding your pain with the clinical screen, or go home whenever you like.
onboarding.beliefsSkipHint: You can resume these questions in the screening whenever you want.
onboarding.neuroWhat: Your nervous system is not fixed. It learns, adapts, and changes with experience — that is neuroplasticity. It can learn to protect you with more alertness… and it can also learn, little by little, safer ways to move, rest, and live.
onboarding.neuroPain: In chronic pain, the body sometimes keeps sending danger signals even when the original threat is no longer the same. That does not mean it is all in your head. It means the brain and spinal cord take part in how pain is felt — and that this can be worked with respect, evidence, and patience.
onboarding.bpsBody: Pain does not live only in one tissue. It lives alongside sleep, stress, relationships, movement, medication, and the stories you tell yourself. Looking at those pieces together — body, mind, and context — is the integrative approach: not to blame you, but to open real paths to relief and function.
onboarding.neuroFootnote: Neuropi (biopsychosocial / neuroplasticity approach) guides and educates. It does not diagnose or replace your care team.

assessment.title: Screening
assessment.pickerHint: Short modules in clinical order: pain, IASP mechanisms, intensity, lifestyle pillars, medications, mood, and stress. You can pause — progress is saved.
assessment.psychWhy: At the end we orient why pain psychotherapy may fit your profile — useful for many, to discuss with your care team.
assessment.mechanismBody: We use “pattern compatible with…” language (nociceptive, neuropathic, nociplastic, or mixed). We never diagnose a mechanism; mechanisms can coexist.
assessment.mechanismPending: Complete the IASP module for a clearer orientation.
assessment.whyPsychIndicated: Your profile suggests exploring pain psychotherapy with your care team: beliefs, interference, or mechanisms that often benefit from CBT/ACT for pain, alongside medical care. Neuropi orients; it does not prescribe treatments.
assessment.whyPsychGeneral: Although each case differs, in persistent pain psychotherapy often helps with function, fear of movement, and automatic thoughts — without denying that pain is real. It is often part of integrated care, not a luxury.

psych.title: Pain psychotherapy
psych.intro: Pain psychotherapy does not deny that pain is physical. It helps you live with less fear, more function, and better quality of life — and for many profiles it is often a useful piece of integrated care.
psych.validates: Your pain is real. Psychological work does not mean “it is all in your head”.
psych.whenHelps: It can help when pain limits life, there is fear of movement, automatic thoughts, high stress, or you want a plan beyond medication.
